parts:
The good news is that nothing is actually behind anymore. All the ChatGPT work from your other computer (Oct 4–10: prime-variance-exponents, exponent descent, newman collisions, through `537e408` this morning) is in `origin/main`, and it's in your local `main` too — the pull of `main` on this machine worked fine. The only thing that went wrong was the pull on `claude-investigation`, which tried to rebase onto a remote copy of that branch frozen on Sept 30.

What this machine has that GitHub doesn't is small and purely additive: the Sept 30 character-channels investigation, the Oct 1 round-2 Sonin review files you committed this morning (`9083ceb`, four new files, nothing overwritten), and the merge commit tying them together. So the fix is just to publish `main` and stop the stale branch from biting you again. I can't push from here (the sandbox can't reach GitHub over SSH), so from a terminal on this computer:

```
git push origin main
git push --force-with-lease origin claude-investigation
git config pull.rebase false
```

The second line is only needed if you want to keep `claude-investigation` on GitHub; since it's now identical to `main`, you could instead delete it (`git branch -d claude-investigation` and `git push origin --delete claude-investigation`) and avoid the stale-branch problem entirely — I'd lean that way. The third line makes future pulls merge rather than rebase, which is what caused today's mess.

Then on the other computer, a plain `git pull` on `main` brings it up to date, with no conflicts expected since everything new is additive.

parts: My other computer is on a new branch now though, so how do I get the changes into that branch there?

metadata.source: Claude Cowork session event, completed public message

parts:
Once you've pushed `main` from this computer, on the other machine, with your new branch checked out:

```
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
```

That brings everything from `main` into your new branch as a merge commit, leaving the branch's own commits intact. Because the only things `main` gained are new files (the character-channels folder, the four round-2 Sonin review files, and the `papers/investigations/README.md` index), there shouldn't be conflicts unless your new branch has also created files at those exact paths. If it does conflict and you want main's version, `git checkout --theirs <file>` then `git add <file>` and `git commit` finishes it.

One thing to check first on that machine: run `git status` and make sure the branch started from a recent `main` (its `git log` should show `537e408 More work on newman collisions...` in its history). If it branched off an older point, the merge above still works, it'll just pull in more.

Also, if that computer has `pull.rebase=true` set as well, I'd run `git config pull.rebase false` there too, since the same stale-branch rebase could happen whenever your new branch gets pushed and later diverges.
